title: Psalm 63: My Soul Thirsts for You
summary: In the dry wilderness of Judah, David longs for God as a parched body longs for water. Remembering God's power and glory in the sanctuary, he declares that God's loving devotion is better than life itself, and he meditates on God through the night. The psalm ends with confidence that his enemies will fall and the king will rejoice in God.
story: Psalm 63 is the last of the Davidic psalms in Book II with a historical heading, and it takes us once more into the wilderness where David spent so much of his life. It belongs with the trust psalms of 61 to 64, but its tone is closer to longing than to lament. The psalmist's desire is not first for rescue but for God himself. It echoes Psalm 42, which opened Book II with a deer panting for water, and it gives Book II one of its most intimate prayers. Christians have long treated it as a morning prayer, and in many traditions it has been sung at dawn.
historical:
The heading places David “in the Wilderness of Judah,” the dry, rugged country between the hills of Judah and the Dead Sea. David spent time there in two periods of his life. As a young man he fled from Saul and hid in the wilderness strongholds of Ziph, Maon, and En-gedi (1 Samuel 23 to 24). Later, as king, he fled from Absalom's rebellion, crossing the Kidron Valley and heading toward the wilderness on the way to the Jordan (2 Samuel 15:23-28; 16:2). Because verse 11 speaks of “the king,” many interpreters favor the flight from Absalom, when David was already king and was cut off from the sanctuary where the ark had been left behind in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:25). Others connect it with the earlier period and take the reference to the king as David's confidence in his anointing, or as a later addition for liturgical use.

As with the other historical headings, scholars differ on whether it records the original occasion or was added by editors who saw the psalm's wilderness imagery and connected it with David's story. The Greek translation of the Old Testament renders the verb in verse 1 with a word meaning to rise early, and that reading helped make the psalm a morning prayer in Christian worship.
cultural:
The Judean wilderness receives very little rain, and its wadis run dry for much of the year. A person traveling through it without water would quickly be in danger. When David speaks of his body yearning “in a dry and weary land without water,” he describes a physical reality, not just a figure of speech.

Verse 5 speaks of the “richest of foods,” literally fat and fatness. Fat was considered the choicest part of a meal and of a sacrifice (Leviticus 3:16 says all the fat belongs to the LORD), and a feast with rich food was a sign of abundance and celebration. Verse 6 refers to the watches of the night. Israel divided the night into watches, periods when guards took turns (Judges 7:19; Lamentations 2:19), and lying awake through them meant a sleepless night. Lifting the hands (verse 4) was a common posture of prayer and praise. The foxes of verse 10 are probably jackals, scavengers that fed on the bodies of the dead after a battle; to become their portion meant dying without burial, a disgrace in the ancient world.
literary: The psalm moves from longing to satisfaction to confidence. Verses 1 and 2 describe thirst and memory: David has seen God in the sanctuary and now seeks him in the wilderness. Verses 3 to 5 turn to praise, centered on the claim that God's loving devotion is better than life. Verses 6 to 8 describe night meditation and clinging to God. Verses 9 to 11 shift to the enemies and the king's joy. The imagery moves from thirst to feasting, from dry land to rich food. Verse 8 holds two movements together: the soul clings to God, and God's right hand holds the soul. The same pairing of human seeking and divine holding runs through the whole psalm.

outline.t: Thirsting for God in a dry land
Loving devotion better than life, a soul satisfied
Remembering God through the night, held by his hand
The king will rejoice in God

doctrines.note: The psalm begins, “O God, You are my God.” Its whole longing is for God himself, not first for his gifts. God is shown to be the soul's true good, more valuable than life itself.
David seeks God earnestly, remembers him at night, and lifts his hands in praise. Prayer here is desire and attention, a turning of the whole person, body and soul, toward God.
God's loving devotion is called better than life. His covenant love is the highest good the psalmist knows, and it is the reason for his praise.

words.note: Shachar, to seek earnestly. It is related to the noun for dawn, and some interpreters think it carries the sense of seeking early, at first light. The Greek translation took it that way. The verb expresses intense, eager searching.

Tsame, to thirst. In verse 1 the soul thirsts for God. The same image appears in Psalm 42:2 and in the invitation of Isaiah 55:1. Thirst is the most urgent of bodily needs, and the psalm uses it to describe the soul's need for God.

Davaq, to cling, to stick to. It is the verb of Genesis 2:24, where a man clings to his wife, and of Ruth 1:14, where Ruth clings to Naomi. In verse 8 the soul clings to God, a picture of loyal, close attachment.

Chesed, loving devotion or steadfast love. In verse 3 it is better than life. The claim is striking: God's covenant love is valued more than survival itself, which puts all the psalm's longing in perspective.

christ: Jesus spoke of a thirst for God that he himself satisfies: whoever believes in him will never be thirsty (John 6:35), and whoever is thirsty may come to him and drink (John 7:37). The psalm's longing for God in a dry land finds its answer in him. Jesus also went into the wilderness and faced hunger and testing there, trusting God's word rather than bread (Matthew 4:1-4). The New Testament does not quote Psalm 63 directly, so the connections are thematic, but the psalm's claim that God's loving devotion is better than life finds a new depth in Christ, who gave his life out of love and whose love, Paul says, nothing in life or death can separate us from (Romans 8:38-39).
questions: David says God's loving devotion is better than life. What would it mean for you to value God's love that highly?
When you lie awake at night, what fills your mind? How might remembering God change those hours?
The psalm describes both clinging to God and being held by him. Which of these do you need to hear more today?
